# Where we are

## A question we kept deferring

Consequentialism said the right act is the one that makes the outcome best.

. . .

Deontology said no, some things are off limits whatever the outcome.

. . .

Both of them owe us an account of what makes an outcome *good* in the first place. The consequentialist needs it to state the theory at all. The deontologist needs it to say what the rules are protecting.

## Mill's answer

:::: {.callout-note title="Mill, *Utilitarianism*, ch. 2"}
By happiness is intended pleasure, and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain, and the privation of pleasure.
::::

. . .

We let that go by in week nine. It is a substantive, contestable claim, and for the next four classes it's the thing under examination.

## Four classes on one question

Today
:    What are we even asking? Fixing the question before trying to answer it.

Thursday
:    Hedonism. Mill's answer, pressed hard.

Next week
:    Desire theories, then objective lists. And then: who gets to have a welfare at all?

## Why this isn't bookkeeping

Suppose you're allocating a fixed hospital budget. Or deciding whether a policy that leaves people richer but lonelier is an improvement.

. . .

You can't answer either without a view about what makes someone's life go better. "Whatever they'd choose" is a view. So is "whatever makes them report feeling good."

. . .

Those are different views, and they come apart in exactly the cases where the money is.

# The concept

## Good, and good for

A Vermeer is a good painting. It's beautiful, it's quiet, it rewards looking at for a long time.

. . .

None of that is good *for* the painting. There is nothing it is like to be a painting. Nothing goes well or badly from its point of view, because it hasn't got one.

. . .

Welfare is the *good for* relation: how well a life goes for the one living it.

## Not the same as being good

You can be a good person and have a miserable life. You can be a scoundrel and have a wonderful one.

. . .

How often those combinations actually occur is a real question, and one the Greeks cared about enormously. But they're clearly possible, and possible is enough to show the two notions come apart.

. . .

Philosophers sometimes call welfare **prudential** value, to keep it clear of moral value and of aesthetic value.

## It can go below zero

Welfare isn't a measure of how much good stuff a life contains. It can be negative.

. . .

Someone in unrelieved pain, with no prospect of relief, has a life that is going badly *for them* — on some views, worse than no life at all.

. . .

Whatever theory you end up with has to allow that. A theory that can only ever add things up will not.

## Why not just say "happiness"?

In ordinary English, happiness is a mood. You can be happy this afternoon and not this evening.

. . .

Welfare is about how a life goes across its whole length. A life can go well without being one long good mood, and a string of good moods doesn't obviously add up to a life that went well.

. . .

"Flourishing" is the other candidate, but it carries the suggestion that there's a way humans are *supposed* to grow, like a plant toward light. Some people hold that. It shouldn't be smuggled in by the vocabulary.

## Fixing the question first

Notice what we have not done. We haven't said what makes a life go well.

. . .

We've only said what we're asking about: the things that are good for the person whose life it is.

. . .

That separation earns its keep. People with wildly different theories can agree on the question. If they couldn't, they'd be talking past each other rather than disagreeing.

## A moment, or a life

Two different questions hide inside "how is it going for her?"

. . .

There's how things are for her *right now* — this afternoon, in this mood, in this room.

. . .

And there's how her life is going, taken whole. Those come apart. A miserable afternoon in the middle of a good life is both a miserable afternoon and a good life.

. . .

Most of the theories we'll see are built to answer the second question and then say something about the first as a consequence. It's worth noticing which way round a theory does it.

# Three families

## Three families of answer

Hedonism
:    Welfare is pleasure, and the absence of pain. Nothing else counts on its own.

Desire theories
:    Welfare is getting what you want. What you want doesn't matter; the wanting does.

Objective lists
:    Some things are good for you whether or not you want them, and whether or not they feel good.

. . .

Those are the next three classes. They aren't the only options, but nearly everything else is a variation on one, or a combination of two.

## What actually divides them

The deep split isn't three ways, it's two.

Subjective
:    Something is good for you *because of* your attitude to it. You wanted it, or it felt good. Change the attitude and you change the value.

Objective
:    Some things are good for you whether or not you have any attitude toward them at all.

. . .

Hedonism and desire theories are both on the subjective side, for all that they disagree. Objective lists are on the other side by themselves.

## The hard constraint

Here's what the objective theorist is up against.

. . .

It seems wrong to say something is good *for* someone if it leaves them entirely cold — if they get nothing from it, never wanted it, and never would have.

. . .

That thought is most of the case for subjective theories, and it is a strong one. The objective theorist has to either satisfy it or explain it away. We'll watch them try on the 12th.

## iClicker POLL

Two lives, the same length.

In the first, someone is mildly content from beginning to end. Nothing much happens. Nothing goes wrong.

In the second, someone works at something hard, fails a great deal, and eventually makes something they care about.

Which goes better *for the person living it*?

A.  The first
B.  The second
C.  Exactly as well as each other
D.  There's no fact of the matter

## What that was testing

If you said A, you're being pulled toward something in the neighborhood of hedonism.

. . .

If you said B, you think something other than how it feels from the inside is making a difference. That's what objective list theories say.

. . .

If you said C, you may be a desire theorist, depending on what the two of them wanted.

. . .

And if you said D, you owe the rest of us an account of what we've been arguing about.

## One more question, in the background

We keep saying *a person's* welfare. The concept doesn't obviously stop at people.

. . .

A dog can have a life that goes well or badly for the dog. Can a fish? A bee? A language model?

. . .

We come back to that on the 12th. The answer turns out to depend on which of the three theories you take, which is a good sign that the three are doing real work.
